P1.evidence: No setter, so P1a does not apply. The rep opened directly from the inbound application — 'I've seen your application, but I would love to hear it from you, like the story behind it, and what you're trying to fix right now with your fitness, with your health, and how can we potentially help you with it?' — which is a clean open question and drew an immediately honest answer. The frame carried only two of four parts and no agreement was sought. The cost is measurable at 01:37:18, where the price landed as audible shock: 'Whoa... I wasn't expecting that.' Nothing in the opening told this prospect a purchase decision was on the table today.

P2.evidence: Work was covered well and used later — software engineer, three days in the office and two at home, standing desk, and the sitting the rep connected to the back pain. Training week asked and quantified at three days, with a good follow-up on why three rather than more, which surfaced his real fear: 'I don't want to be overwhelmed to avoid quitting.' Diet asked properly and walked through. Against that: no age asked (40 was volunteered), no height, no weight — on a prospect whose central problem is that his body weighs too much for him to move it. No health-conditions question at all. Injuries scores partial only because the prospect raised the back and knees himself; the rep then followed up well, asking when the knees flare and at what activities, which produced the toe-walking gait explanation. Sleep and daytime energy were both skipped entirely.

P3.evidence: The what-becomes-possible question ran in an unusually good form — 'when you think about yourself, like in six months, 12 months from now, when you're actually achieving that, what does become possible?' — and produced the best answer of the call: basketball again after five years, easier skating, less suffering on hikes, and then the line that should be quoted back to him at every check-in, 'wearing socks were something that was very difficult because the belly is fat... sometimes I was like, I was suffocating. So, yeah, I will be able to move in my body, breathe, walk, play with kids. Just live.' The rep's reflect-back was short but correct: 'Just living without pain.' The who-else layer ran properly too — 'Do you have kids?' into the six-year-old gymnast and 'how's your back responding to that?' — which tied the pain to the relationship. No aesthetics question was asked and no explicit bridge question, though the what-becomes-possible framing did much of the same work.

P4.evidence: The phase never ran. Nobody asked what he had tried, what happened with it, or why it did not stick, even though he volunteered the headline — 'I abandoned myself a little bit for some years' — and even though he is currently mid-restart and hating it. The nearest thing to a blocker question was the rep asking why three sessions rather than more, which surfaced the fear of being overwhelmed and quitting. That is genuinely useful and it was left there. This is the weakest P4 in the batch, and on a prospect whose entire risk profile is quitting again it was the phase most worth running.

P5.evidence: Never run, for the twelfth consecutive call in this batch. The material was unusually strong and unusually easy to reach for: a 40-year-old who cannot lift his own body weight, struggles to put socks on, has daily back pain and a six-year-old who wants to be thrown in the air. A single question about what that looks like in two years if nothing changes would have carried real weight against a tax bill.

P6.evidence: The all-in question ran in full scripted form with the identity hook tailored to what he had said: 'if we can figure out all the details, like the financials and so on, are you fully committed to actually showing up and doing the necessary work to become that version of Yannick that finally picks up basketball after five years?' The answer was unambiguous — 'I'm really, I'm locked in this movement. So yeah, I spent so many years on the side and I don't want it anymore.' A clear yes was banked before the price. The belief question proper was never asked separately; the earlier 'do you feel like this kind of approach would actually work for you?' drew a mild 'Yeah, I like it', which is why P6a is partial.

P11.evidence: None of the four steps completed. No payment. No onboarding call with Trevor. No agreement. No welcome sequence. The rep offered to send the Payva link so the prospect could check availability himself, but no send is confirmed. The call ends with the prospect leaving to build a spreadsheet.

objection_plays.detail: The trigger was visible before it was spoken and the rep read it correctly: 'I saw your reaction. So I understand like putting it all up front would be a stretch.' He then ran one financial-picture move better than anywhere else in this batch — asking outright for the number rather than dancing around it: 'what's your cache right now that you could put right now, so the rest we can split?' drawing a real answer, 'I would say maximum 2K'. That is the move working as designed. From there it stalls. No isolation was run at any point, so the rep never established that money was the only obstacle. No should-versus-how frame. No monthly surplus, no cards, no available credit, no investments, and critically no credit score — which matters because financing was the main route he was pushing. And when the three-pay was declined, the rep did not counter with the hybrid the prospect had himself floated ($2,000 down, $4,000 financed); he let him leave to do the arithmetic alone.

Trigger was clear — a tax bill in two months, a need to model the budget, and 'I need to be sure to be able to sustain that effort for 12 months.' Not one OD move ran. No things-never-slow-down, no when-does-it-become-the-right-time, no compounding-cost, no 'what if all you had to do was show up'. Partially mitigated by the tightest recall in the batch: the rep booked the next day rather than next month, which is the right instinct even without the scripted moves.

A fear trigger sat in plain sight from early in the call and was never treated as one: 'I'm in that phase where I hate my training because everything is painful, everything is hard, my body weighs a ton', and later the reason he caps himself at three sessions — 'I don't want to be overwhelmed to avoid quitting.' That is a man afraid he will fail again. No OE move ran: no certainty question, no pleasure-versus-pain, no bridge, no plane, no burned-before, no 'how will you know if you never actually try'. The rep did reassure him that the first sessions would be hard and not to be discouraged, which is useful but generic. Given quitting is the single largest risk to this deal and to delivery, this was the play to run.

SCRIPT GAP — a prospect outside the stated ICP on the exclusion criterion. The ICP quote explicitly excludes people who are substantially overweight and struggling, and this prospect describes being unable to lift his own body weight, finding every session painful, and having struggled to put socks on because of abdominal fat. There is no scripted disqualification path and no guidance on whether such a prospect should be steered to the self-paced product, so the rep ran the standard $6,000 pitch. Note the inconsistency this creates across the batch: a five-of-five ICP match was proactively downsold three days earlier on the Nik Howe call, while this prospect, who fails four criteria, was pitched the flagship.

SCRIPT GAP — international payments. The prospect is in France and knows the local consumer finance market better than the rep does, citing Klarna's French terms. The rep could not compare, could not spell the provider name reliably, and could not confirm whether Payva serves French customers at all, ultimately deferring: 'I will send you the link, so you can actually check it out.' The primary payment route offered to this buyer may simply not be available to him, and nothing in the playbook covers non-US payment options.

notes: P6 ran completely and got a genuine yes, and the rep asked the single best cash question in the batch — what can you actually put down now — and got a real number. Everything around it failed. P4 did not run at all on a prospect whose defining risk is quitting again, P5 did not run for the twelfth consecutive call, and no isolation was ever attempted, so nobody established whether money was really the only obstacle. Two items for the principal rather than the coach: this prospect sits outside the stated ICP on the exclusion criterion and was pitched the flagship anyway, three days after a perfect-fit prospect was proactively downsold; and the rep is offering a US financing product to a French buyer without knowing whether it serves him.
